candidates.statement: FDA has received an increasing number of questions regarding the extent to which generally 17 accepted scientific knowledge (GASK) may be relied on for drug or biological product 18 approval. 2 This guidance describes instances in which it may be appropriate to rely on GASK to 19 meet certain nonclinical safety requirements for new drug applications (NDAs) submitted under 20 section 505(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 355(b)) and 21 biologics license applications (BLAs) under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act (PHS 22 Act) (42 U.S.C. 262(a)). The information that supports the nonclinical safety of a drug and that 23 must be submitted in the application can include references to GASK, when appropriate, instead 24 of or in addition to, specific studies conducted with respect to the drug. In such cases, therefore, 25 it might be unnecessary to conduct certain nonclinical studies. 3
candidates.context: This guidance focuses on two examples of GASK that could be appropriate to fulfill certain legal 28 and regulatory requirements applicable to the drug or biological product in question. The 29 examples discussed in this guidance reflect areas where we have previously determined that it 30 was appropriate to rely on GASK to meet certain requirements for approval. Notably, while the 31 examples provided here are for illustrative purposes, determinations regarding the 32 appropriateness of data submitted for any application, including GASK, are fact-specific, and the 33 question of whether certain information can be considered GASK and the purpose such 34 information would serve in an application will be considered in the context of a particular 35 application. 36

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 38 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 39 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 40 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 41 not required. 42

candidates.statement: Standalone marketing applications submitted under section 505(b)(1) of the FD&C Act or 85 section 351(a) of the PHS Act must contain data sufficient to demonstrate the safety and 86 effectiveness of the drug, or the safety, purity, and potency of the biological product, 87 respectively. As a general matter, applicants for standalone marketing applications rely on either 88 their own data or data to which they have a right of reference. A standalone application’s 89 nonclinical data (which, as discussed above, may be derived from in vitro or in vivo studies, as 90 appropriate) thus generally come from two potential sources: studies conducted by the sponsor 91 and studies not conducted by or for the sponsor but to which the sponsor has a right of reference. 92 In some instances, such as in those circumstances described in this guidance with regard to 93 nonclinical data, it may also be appropriate in a standalone marketing application to rely on 94 information that is considered GASK to support approval without affecting the regulatory status 95 of standalone marketing applications submitted under section 505(b)(1) of the FD&C Act or 96 section 351(a) of the PHS Act. Similarly, marketing applications submitted under section 97 505(b)(2) of the FD&C Act or section 351(k) of the PHS Act may rely on information that is 98 considered GASK to support approval. 99

Some drugs have as their active ingredient a substance that is naturally present in the human 149 body — for example, in situations where the drug replaces a substance that should naturally be 150 present but, for pathological reasons, a patient may lack sufficient amounts of the substance to 151 enable proper functioning. In those cases, where the drug is an unmodified 13 endogenous 152 substance and a patient’s exposure to the drug reflects the same level of exposure and 153 distribution of the endogenous substance seen in a healthy individual, GASK regarding the safety 154 of such a drug may be used to obviate the need for certain nonclinical data. 155
